params.alt: Three reasons DEI matters in research: more than fairness, more representative knowledge, better innovation. DEI is both an ethical responsibility and a scientific necessity.

params.text:
Research That Includes Everyone

In today's increasingly interconnected and diverse world, Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) are essential principles in conducting ethical and impactful research. DEI in research is about more than fairness: it ensures that all individuals, regardless of background, have equal opportunities to participate in and benefit from scientific discovery.

By embracing DEI, researchers create a more representative and robust body of knowledge, addressing the needs and experiences of diverse communities and fostering innovation.

Fostering DEI is not just an ethical responsibility but a necessity for producing impactful, credible and socially relevant knowledge. By actively considering DEI, researchers can avoid biases, ensure equitable representation and create inclusive practices that enhance the quality, applicability and trustworthiness of their findings.

Watch: What Is DEI in Research?

This short video explains why DEI matters in research and defines diversity, equity and inclusion. Captions are off by default: click the CC button in the player to turn them on.

params.alt: The module audience: Research Ethics Committee members (new and experienced) and researchers (early-career, mid-career and senior), plus institutional leaders.

params.text:
Who Is This Module For?

These groups will benefit from tailored, accessible content that enhances their knowledge, compliance practices and decision-making in research ethics, contributing to a more inclusive and responsible research community.

Research Ethics Committee (REC) members

  • Members who review and oversee research projects to ensure ethical standards are met, including new REC members who may benefit from structured, foundational training.
  • Experienced REC members looking to deepen their understanding of specialised topics, such as AI ethics or digital data ethics.

Researchers

  • Early-career researchers (postgraduate students, PhD candidates and postdoctoral researchers) who need foundational knowledge in research ethics.
  • Mid-career and senior researchers, especially those engaging with advanced ethical issues in areas like AI, data management and interdisciplinary research.

params.alt: Five learning objectives: understand DEI concepts, identify and mitigate bias, promote inclusive research practices, foster an inclusive research environment, apply DEI in ethics reviews.

params.text:
Purpose and Learning Objectives

This module provides researchers, REC members and institutional leaders with a deeper understanding of DEI principles and their application in research processes.

By the end of this module, participants will be able to:

  • Understand DEI concepts: define diversity, equity and inclusion in research and recognise their ethical implications.
  • Identify and mitigate biases: spot potential sources of bias across research stages and apply strategies to promote fair representation.
  • Promote inclusive research practices: design methodologies that prioritise inclusivity in sampling, participant recruitment and data collection.
  • Foster an inclusive research environment: address structural barriers and advocate for inclusive practices within research teams and institutions.
  • Apply DEI principles in ethics reviews: evaluate proposals with a DEI focus to ensure fair treatment, benefit-sharing and respect for all populations.

metadata.title: 3. What Are Diversity, Equity and Inclusion?
metadata.extraTitle: 3. What Are Diversity, Equity and Inclusion?

params.alt: Definitions: Diversity is the presence of a wide range of characteristics; Equity is fair access with extra support where needed; Inclusion is an environment where all can contribute fully.

params.text:
Three Connected Principles

1. Diversity refers to the presence of a wide range of characteristics and experiences within a team or group. It encompasses various dimensions, such as race, gender, age, ethnicity, sexual orientation, disability and socioeconomic background. In research, diversity enriches the process by bringing in multiple perspectives and insights, ultimately leading to more comprehensive and inclusive findings.

2. Equity ensures that all individuals have fair access to the opportunities, resources and support needed to succeed, recognising that some may require additional assistance to reach the same outcomes as others. In the research context, equity involves proactive efforts to reduce barriers for underrepresented or marginalised groups, promoting a level playing field that benefits the research community and the quality of outcomes.

3. Inclusion is the practice of creating environments where all individuals feel respected, valued and able to contribute fully. In research, inclusion involves integrating diverse voices and perspectives in meaningful ways, ensuring that every team member and study participant is heard and considered. This approach fosters a culture of belonging and respect, leading to richer and more ethical research practices.

params.title: Flip each card to review the key ideas.

dialogs.answer: Having a range of backgrounds, experiences and perspectives, which enriches research and leads to deeper insights and more inclusive findings.
Fair access to opportunities and resources, with extra support where needed to create a level playing field for all team members and participants.
A respectful and open environment where every voice is valued, leading to more ethical practices and research that speaks to a wider audience.

dialogs.text: Why is equity not the same as equality?
dialogs.answer: Equality gives everyone the same; equity recognises that some people need additional assistance to reach the same outcomes.
For example race, gender, age, ethnicity, sexual orientation, disability and socioeconomic background.

metadata.title: 4. DEI in Research Teams and Research Design
metadata.extraTitle: 4. DEI in Research Teams and Research Design

params.alt: How diversity, equity and inclusion apply both to research teams and to research design.

params.text:
Two Arenas for DEI

Incorporating DEI into research teams and research design is essential for creating comprehensive, ethical and impactful studies. Diverse teams bring a range of perspectives, skills and experiences that enhance creativity, improve problem-solving and foster innovation. By embracing equity, research environments can ensure that all members have access to opportunities and resources, promoting fair representation in every phase of the project.

Inclusive research design integrates diverse voices and considerations, leading to studies that reflect and respect the experiences of varied populations. This approach reduces potential biases, increases the relevance of findings and builds trust with the communities affected by research.

  • Diversity. In teams, varied perspectives help address complex challenges and lead to innovative ideas. In design, diversity ensures that studies reflect real-world complexity and consider a wider range of participants, making findings more relevant and inclusive.
  • Equity. In teams, everyone has fair access to opportunities, resources and support, with additional assistance when necessary. In design, equity means actively removing barriers for underrepresented or marginalised groups, so that results do not unfairly favour one group over another.
  • Inclusion. In teams, everyone feels respected, valued and able to contribute ideas. In design, inclusion means intentionally integrating the voices of diverse participants, so that each perspective is considered in the research process.

Together, DEI principles strengthen the foundation of research, making it more meaningful, credible and aligned with societal values.

metadata.title: 5. How DEI Principles Shape Research Design
metadata.extraTitle: 5. How DEI Principles Shape Research Design

params.alt: Four points where DEI shapes research design: framing the question, sampling and recruitment, data collection, analysis and sharing of results.

params.text:
DEI at Every Stage of the Design

Applying DEI principles to research design means asking, at each stage, who is included, who is left out, and who benefits.

  • Framing the question. Whose problem is being studied, and who defined it? Involving affected communities early helps make questions relevant and avoids building the team's own assumptions into the study.
  • Sampling and recruitment. Participant groups should be representative of the population affected by the research. Where some groups are underrepresented, plan ethical steps to reach them.
  • Data collection. Use accessible, culturally and linguistically appropriate instruments, settings and formats, and plan accommodations for participants with disabilities or other specific needs.
  • Analysis and sharing. Where appropriate and lawful, report results for relevant groups rather than only in aggregate, and share findings and benefits with all participant groups, including those historically excluded.

Watch: DEI in Research Design and Bias

This video shows how DEI shapes research design and where bias can enter the research process. Captions are off by default: click the CC button in the player to turn them on.

metadata.title: DEI in Research Design and Bias
metadata.extraTitle: DEI in Research Design and Bias

params.alt: Five common barriers to participation: lack of outreach, cultural and language barriers, restrictive eligibility criteria, historical mistrust, costs and time burdens; and design responses.

params.text:
Barriers to Participation

Underrepresented groups are often missing from research, for example from clinical trials, for reasons that study design can address:

  • Lack of outreach and information
  • Cultural and language barriers
  • Restrictive eligibility criteria
  • Historical mistrust of medical systems
  • Costs and time burdens on participants

Design responses include partnerships with community health centres, bilingual staff, culturally adapted recruitment materials, broader inclusion criteria, flexible scheduling, and compensation and benefits that are fair and culturally appropriate. The Clinical Trials Transformation Initiative stresses that equitable representation in trials is both an ethical and a scientific imperative.

metadata.title: 6. Recognising and Minimising Bias in Research
metadata.extraTitle: 6. Recognising and Minimising Bias in Research

params.alt: Bias can enter at four stages: planning, recruitment, measurement and interpretation.

params.text:
Where Bias Enters

Bias is not only a matter of individual prejudice. It can be built into the way research is planned and carried out:

  • Planning: research questions and hypotheses reflect only the experience and assumptions of a homogeneous team.
  • Recruitment: narrow channels (one notice board, one elite network) and unnecessarily strict criteria exclude underrepresented groups.
  • Measurement: instruments validated in one population are applied uncritically to others, or are not available in accessible formats or relevant languages.
  • Interpretation: the majority group is treated as the norm, differences between groups are overlooked, or findings are generalised beyond the people actually studied.
  • Within teams: implicit bias can shape whose contributions are recognised and who is given opportunities.

params.alt: Five strategies to minimise bias: diverse teams, standardised criteria, implicit-bias training, community consultation, monitoring and audits.

params.text:
Strategies to Minimise Bias

  • Build diverse teams that bring different lenses to each stage of the research.
  • Use standardised and transparent criteria for selecting participants, staff and students, and for allocating opportunities.
  • Provide regular implicit-bias training for staff and mentors.
  • Consult the communities concerned, and pilot recruitment materials and instruments with them.
  • Monitor representation throughout the study and audit selection processes.

Knowledge Check

Test your understanding before moving on.

params.question: A team uses a questionnaire validated only with university students in one country to study older adults from several cultural backgrounds. Which type of bias is this most likely to introduce?

answers.text: Measurement bias

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The instrument may not measure the same thing in a different population.

answers.text: Publication bias

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. Publication bias concerns which results get published.

answers.text: Recall bias

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. Recall bias concerns how accurately participants remember past events.

answers.text: No bias, because the instrument is validated

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. Validation in one population does not guarantee validity in another.

params.question: Equity means treating every participant in exactly the same way.

params.alt: Four benefits of diverse research teams: varied lenses, fewer blind spots, more creativity, wider relevance.

params.text:
Why Diverse Teams Do Better Research

Diverse teams bring varied lenses to problem-solving, uncover blind spots, enhance creativity and produce findings that are more widely applicable and cited.

Research on science itself supports this. Large analyses have linked ethnically diverse collaborations with higher citation impact (AlShebli, Rahwan & Woon, 2018), and gender diversity with broader questions and better science under the right conditions (Nielsen et al., 2017). At the same time, underrepresented scientists innovate at higher rates but see their novel contributions discounted (Hofstra et al., 2020): a reminder that diversity must come with fair recognition.

Additional material: the infographics referred to in the module source, "Strategic & financial benefits of a diverse workforce" (Transcend) and "Starting points for increasing DEI in your research" (Wiley), are linked in the References chapter.

params.alt: Diversity without inclusion versus inclusion in practice: sharing leadership, authorship and visible roles.

params.text:
From Presence to Participation

DEI is not just about who is present, but also about power dynamics and inclusion in decision-making. A team can look diverse while junior or underrepresented members are excluded from major decisions, authorship and visible roles such as conference presentations.

Assigning presentations and authorship only to senior members excludes junior or underrepresented members from critical career-building opportunities, perpetuates power imbalances and undermines the team's diversity of thought. Inclusion in practice means sharing leadership, authorship and visibility, mentoring actively, and recognising lived experiences and diverse epistemologies as assets.

params.alt: Inclusive recruitment checklist in three stages: before, during and after recruitment.

params.text:
Checklist for Inclusive Recruitment in Research Teams

Use this checklist when recruiting research staff, students or collaborators. Open each stage below to see the full list.

• Define diversity and inclusion goals for the team (e.g. gender balance, representation of minority groups).
  • Review job descriptions and role criteria for biased language or unnecessary requirements.
  • Ensure that recruitment materials use inclusive language and imagery.
  • Plan outreach to diverse networks (cultural organisations, professional associations, community groups).
  • Set up a diverse hiring panel to review candidates and conduct interviews.

• Advertise roles widely, not only in elite or limited spaces (e.g. mainstream job boards, community boards, academic diversity groups).
  • Offer flexible application processes (e.g. remote interview options, alternative formats for submitting portfolios).
  • Ensure interview questions are standardised and focused on skills and competencies, not cultural fit alone.
  • Provide clear information about the organisation's DEI commitments.

• Document diversity outcomes of the recruitment process (track applicant demographics where legally appropriate).
  • Conduct a post-recruitment review to identify barriers or improvements.
  • Provide onboarding that highlights inclusive practices and expectations.

params.alt: Everyday inclusion actions for lab leaders, and institution-wide policies that support DEI.

params.text:
Inclusion Day to Day

Lab and team leaders can foster inclusion through simple, regular actions: rotate speaking roles in meetings, ask quieter members for input, recognise contributions publicly and ensure transparent decision-making.

Displaying DEI commitments, such as posters or infographics like IndiaBioscience's "Tenets of our Laboratory", signals that diversity and inclusion are core values, encourages accountability and fosters a sense of belonging for all team members.

Beyond Individual Projects

Institutions support DEI through organisation-wide policies:

  • Leadership commitment to DEI
  • Allocation of resources and staff training
  • Partnerships with communities
  • Systematic data collection and benchmarking

In Europe, institutional Gender Equality Plans (GEPs) provide one such framework for building balanced teams.

params.alt: Useful DEI metrics compared with ineffective interventions that only count uptake.

params.text:
Measuring What Works

Examples of metrics and methods to monitor DEI in research labs include regular audits of recruitment and selection processes (e.g. demographics of applicants and hires), tracking participation and advancement by identity group, and reviewing authorship and presentation allocations.

Not every intervention works. Studies note that generic mentoring or family-friendly policies introduced without measuring impact often report only uptake numbers, rather than showing actual improvements in diversity or inclusion.

metadata.title: 11. Applying DEI Principles in Ethics Reviews
metadata.extraTitle: 11. Applying DEI Principles in Ethics Reviews

params.alt: Four areas for DEI-focused ethics review: representation and sampling, equity in design, inclusion in team processes, ongoing monitoring.

params.text:
A DEI Lens for Ethics Committees

Research Ethics Committees can evaluate proposals with a DEI focus to ensure fair treatment, benefit-sharing and respect for all populations. Four areas help structure the review:

  • Representation and sampling: whether participant groups reflect the population affected, and what might exclude certain groups.
  • Equity in design and implementation: burdens on participants from marginalised groups, fair and culturally appropriate compensation, and accommodations.
  • Inclusion in team processes: whether the team includes relevant perspectives and how all members contribute to decisions.
  • Ongoing monitoring: how DEI is tracked during the study and how findings and benefits reach all participant groups.

These questions complement, rather than replace, the usual review of risks, consent and privacy.

Watch: Applying DEI in Ethics Reviews

This video walks through the four DEI areas that ethics committees can look at. Captions are off by default: click the CC button in the player to turn them on.

metadata.title: 12. Sample DEI Review Questions for Ethics Committees
metadata.extraTitle: 12. Sample DEI Review Questions for Ethics Committees

params.alt: Five sample DEI review questions for ethics committees.

params.text:
Sample DEI Review Questions

Committees and researchers can use these questions when preparing or reviewing a proposal. Open each area to see the questions.

• Are participant groups representative of the population affected by the research?
  • Have you considered barriers (language, culture, accessibility) that might exclude certain groups?
  • What steps will you take to recruit underrepresented populations ethically?

• Does the study design minimise burdens (time, cost, travel) on participants from marginalised groups?
  • Are compensation and benefits equitable and culturally appropriate?
  • Have you planned accommodations for participants with disabilities or other specific needs?

• Does the research team itself include members with varied perspectives relevant to the topic?
  • Are there processes to ensure all team members can contribute to decision-making?
  • How will conflicts around DEI issues be addressed during the project?

• Are there mechanisms to track diversity and inclusion throughout the study?
  • How will findings and benefits be shared with all participant groups, including those historically excluded?
  • Have you planned to review DEI outcomes after the research concludes?

metadata.title: 13. Case Study 1: Promoting Gender Diversity in an AI Research Team
metadata.extraTitle: 13. Case Study 1: Promoting Gender Diversity in an AI Research Team

params.alt: Case study 1: hiring decision for an all-male AI healthcare research team, with ethical issues and suggested resolution.

params.text:
Promoting Gender Diversity in an AI Research Team

Background. A research centre AI team at a leading tech company has been developing machine-learning algorithms for healthcare applications. The team is composed entirely of male researchers and developers, with strong technical expertise but similar perspectives and experiences. The team opens a new Marie Skłodowska-Curie research position to bring in fresh insights. The research centre recently introduced a Gender Equality Plan (GEP) to address gender imbalances, encourage diversity and foster a more inclusive workplace.

Scenario. After an extensive recruitment process, the team is down to its final candidates. Most applicants are male, reflecting the broader gender imbalance in the field. Two stand out: James, who has slightly more experience and technical knowledge in AI applications, and Maria, who is among the strongest candidates and brings a unique background in social sciences and human-centred AI design. Some team members feel James should be chosen for his technical expertise; others argue that hiring Maria would add valuable diversity, especially given her expertise in ethical AI and user-centred design, which could help mitigate biases in their algorithms.

• Prioritising technical skills alone may lead to a lack of diversity in perspectives, which could affect the inclusivity and fairness of the AI models.
  • Hiring decisions could perpetuate gender imbalances if diversity considerations are not part of the process.
  • Balancing the value of technical expertise with the benefits of a diverse and inclusive team environment.

1. How should the hiring committee weigh Maria’s unique skills and perspectives against James’ slightly stronger technical experience?
  2. What are the potential long-term benefits of increasing gender diversity on this AI research team, especially in terms of inclusivity and bias reduction in AI systems?
  3. Should the team consider gender diversity as a formal factor in the hiring process? Why or why not?
  4. How might the team structure its criteria for hiring to value a wider range of skills and perspectives?

The team could consider Maria’s expertise in human-centred AI as a unique and complementary asset that could help address potential biases and improve the ethical dimensions of their work. By bringing in someone with her perspective, the team can benefit from a broader range of skills and insights, ultimately enhancing the inclusivity and fairness of their AI models. Additionally, the organisation could review its hiring criteria in alignment with the Gender Equality Plan to ensure that gender diversity and inclusion are prioritised in decision-making, especially in fields where certain demographics are underrepresented. The GEP provides a framework for building balanced teams that benefit from a broader range of perspectives and contribute to more inclusive research outcomes.

metadata.title: 14. Case Study 2: Increasing Racial and Ethnic Diversity in a Clinical Trials Team
metadata.extraTitle: 14. Case Study 2: Increasing Racial and Ethnic Diversity in a Clinical Trials Team

params.alt: Case study 2: under-enrolment of Black, Hispanic and Asian participants in a cardiovascular trial, with ethical issues and suggested resolution.

params.text:
Increasing Racial and Ethnic Diversity in a Clinical Trials Team

Background. A university hospital is coordinating a multi-site clinical trial on a new cardiovascular treatment. The research team, composed primarily of white clinicians and scientists, has struggled to recruit participants from Black, Hispanic and Asian communities, despite evidence that these populations have a higher prevalence of the target disease. Guidance from the Clinical Trials Transformation Initiative stresses the ethical and scientific imperative to ensure equitable representation in trials.

Scenario. Enrolment numbers are skewed. Community feedback highlights mistrust, cultural barriers and a lack of targeted outreach. A senior investigator proposes partnering with local community health centres, hiring bilingual staff and revising inclusion criteria to accommodate broader participation. Some colleagues argue that these steps will increase costs and delay the timeline; others insist they are essential to achieving generalisable results.

• Limiting diversity may perpetuate inequities in treatment outcomes.
  • Institutional practices may unintentionally favour already-privileged groups.
  • Balancing resource allocation and deadlines with the moral duty to be inclusive.

1. What recruitment strategies could ensure equitable participation without compromising scientific rigour?
  2. How might community partnerships improve trust and outcomes?
  3. Should the team advocate for organisational-level diversity policies to support future trials?

Implement partnerships with community clinics, culturally adapted recruitment materials and regular staff training on implicit bias. Funders and institutions should recognise these efforts as integral, not optional, and incorporate them into policy. This approach supports both ethical integrity and better science.

metadata.title: 15. Case Study 3: Balancing Gender and Rank in a Social Science Research Group
metadata.extraTitle: 15. Case Study 3: Balancing Gender and Rank in a Social Science Research Group

params.alt: Case study 3: senior faculty keep authorship and presentations for themselves in a diverse social science group.

params.text:
Balancing Gender and Rank in a Social Science Research Group

Background. A sociology department at a predominantly white institution launches a project on intersectional justice. The team includes junior faculty (mostly women and BIPOC) and senior faculty (mostly white men). The juniors raise concerns about being excluded from major decision-making and authorship discussions, despite contributing critical insights. The literature emphasises that DEI is not just about who is present but also about power dynamics and inclusion in decision-making.

Scenario. During a planning meeting, senior investigators assign writing tasks and conference presentations exclusively to other senior colleagues. When questioned, they argue these assignments require "experience" and "reputation". Junior team members feel sidelined and worry that their perspectives, particularly on the racialised and gendered dimensions of the research, will be diluted.

• Superficial diversity without genuine inclusion undermines team equity.
  • Hierarchical norms can reinforce systemic barriers.
  • Lack of mentorship and credit-sharing jeopardises early-career researchers’ advancement.

1. How can teams actively distribute opportunities for leadership and authorship?
  2. What structures (e.g. rotating roles, transparent criteria) could reduce rank-based bias?
  3. How should grievances about power dynamics be addressed?

Introduce transparent workload and authorship policies, and rotate key tasks (conference presentations, first-authorship slots) among team members. Senior faculty should mentor juniors actively, acknowledging that lived experiences and diverse epistemologies are assets, not barriers.

params.question: Why is assigning conference presentations and authorship only to senior members a DEI issue?

answers.text: It excludes junior or underrepresented members from career-building opportunities, perpetuates power imbalances and undermines diversity of thought.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct.

answers.text: It is not a DEI issue, because seniority is a neutral criterion.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. In this team, rank closely follows gender and race, so "neutral" criteria reproduce inequity.

answers.text: It only matters if the junior members complain formally.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. The structural issue exists regardless of formal complaints.

answers.text: It is a DEI issue only for the conference organisers.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. The team controls how its own opportunities are shared.

metadata.title: 16. Case Study 4: Creating an Inclusive Undergraduate Research Lab
metadata.extraTitle: 16. Case Study 4: Creating an Inclusive Undergraduate Research Lab

params.alt: Case study 4: an undergraduate psychology lab with narrow recruitment, and how to open it up.

params.text:
Creating an Inclusive Undergraduate Research Lab

Background. A psychology department is known for high-impact research, but its lab assistants are predominantly from high-income, white backgrounds. Underrepresented students (first-generation, lower-income, racial minorities) often assume they "don’t belong". Studies show that inclusive recruitment and retention practices, such as proactive outreach and flexible scheduling, improve diversity and student success in labs.

Scenario. The lab advertises openings on a single bulletin board in the honours lounge, where few underrepresented students go. When one student of colour applies, peers unintentionally question their qualifications. A faculty mentor proposes new outreach (through cultural clubs, diverse imagery in recruitment materials and assurances of flexible hours). Some lab members worry this may "lower standards", while others highlight research on how diverse teams yield stronger findings.

• Narrow recruitment channels reinforce exclusivity.
  • Implicit bias can deter capable applicants.
  • Fair access to research opportunities is key to academic equity.

1. What outreach and selection practices would attract and support diverse applicants?
  2. How can mentors counteract bias in selection and evaluation?
  3. Should research labs formally monitor their diversity efforts?

Adopt inclusive recruitment materials featuring diverse students, advertise across campus networks (cultural clubs, advising centres) and audit selection criteria for bias. Faculty mentors should lead bias-awareness sessions and track diversity metrics annually to ensure accountability.

params.question: Widening outreach to cultural clubs and advising centres necessarily lowers the lab’s selection standards.

params.alt: Four lessons across the case studies: widen the search, make criteria explicit, share power, measure and adjust.

params.text:
What the Cases Teach

  • Widen the search. Narrow channels, such as a single bulletin board or an elite network, produce narrow teams and narrow samples.
  • Make criteria explicit. Transparent criteria for hiring, workload and authorship reduce bias based on rank or identity.
  • Share power. Inclusion means voice, credit and leadership, not just presence.
  • Measure and adjust. Track outcomes over time and treat DEI efforts as integral to good research, not optional extras.

params.title: Key terms of DEI in research

dialogs.answer: The presence of individuals with different identities, backgrounds and perspectives.
Fair access to opportunities, recognising that some groups need additional support to reach the same level.
Ensuring that all team members and participants feel valued, heard and able to contribute fully.
Groups whose share in a team, field or study is smaller than their share in the relevant population.
Unconscious attitudes or stereotypes that affect understanding, actions and decisions.
An institutional plan setting out commitments and actions to promote gender equality, e.g. in recruitment and career progression.
The way social categories such as gender, race and class overlap and combine to shape experiences of advantage or disadvantage.
Making sure that the findings and benefits of research reach all participant groups, including those historically excluded.

params.question: Diverse teams tend to produce findings that are more widely applicable and cited, because they bring varied lenses, uncover blind spots and enhance creativity.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. Transparent decision-making supports inclusion.

answers.text: Recognise only the final results, not individual contributions.

params.alt: Key takeaways: understand DEI as an ethical and scientific necessity; design and review with DEI in mind; include through shared voice, credit and leadership.

params.text:
Key Takeaways

  • DEI is both an ethical responsibility and a scientific necessity for impactful, credible and socially relevant research.
  • Diversity is who is present; equity is fair access with support where needed; inclusion is whether every voice counts.
  • DEI shapes every stage of research design, from framing the question to sharing results, and bias can enter at each of them.
  • Diverse teams do better research, but only with genuine inclusion: shared voice, credit and leadership.
  • Inclusive recruitment, everyday inclusion and institutional policies need monitoring to show that they work.
  • Ethics committees can apply a DEI lens to representation, equity in design, team processes and ongoing monitoring.
Diversity, equity and inclusion apply to both research teams and research design.
Ask who is included, who is left out and who benefits at every stage; use diverse teams, transparent criteria, training and monitoring against bias.
Use the inclusive recruitment checklist before, during and after recruitment; share opportunities and credit.
Use the sample DEI review questions alongside the usual review of risks, consent and privacy.
Widen the search, make criteria explicit, share power, measure and adjust.
Small, deliberate changes in recruitment, design and team practice add up to research that is fairer, more trustworthy and more useful to society.

Key Texts

  • Ahmad, A. S., Sabat, I., Trump-Steele, R. & King, E. (2019). Evidence-based strategies for improving diversity and inclusion in undergraduate research labs. Frontiers in Psychology, 10, 1305. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.01305
  • Chambers, D., Preston, L., Topakas, A., de Saille, S., Salway, S., Booth, A., Dawson, J. & Wilsdon, J. (2017). Review of diversity and inclusion literature and an evaluation of methodologies and metrics relating to health research. Working paper, University of Sheffield, in partnership with the Wellcome Trust.
  • Corneli, A., Hanlen-Rosado, E., McKenna, K., Araojo, R., Corbett, D., Vasisht, K., Siddiqi, B., Johnson, T., Clark, L. T. & Calvert, S. B. (2023). Enhancing diversity and inclusion in clinical trials. Clinical Pharmacology & Therapeutics, 113(3). https://doi.org/10.1002/cpt.2819
  • Dewidar, O., Elmestekawy, N. & Welch, V. (2022). Improving equity, diversity, and inclusion in academia. Research Integrity and Peer Review, 7, 4. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41073-022-00123-z
  • Diversity, equity, and inclusion in research teams: The good, the bad, and the ugly (2022). Race and Justice. https://doi.org/10.1177/21533687221087373
  • Fisher, O. J., Fearnshaw, D., Watson, N. J., Green, P., Charnley, F., McFarlane, D. & Sharples, S. (2024). Promoting equality, diversity and inclusion in research and funding: reflections from a digital manufacturing research network. Research Integrity and Peer Review, 9, 5. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41073-024-00144-w
  • Guyan, K. & Douglas Oloyede, F. (2019). Equality, diversity and inclusion in research and innovation: UK review. Advance HE, for UK Research and Innovation.
  • Keith, K. D. (Ed.) (2011). Cross-Cultural Psychology: Contemporary Themes and Perspectives. Wiley-Blackwell.

Further Reading

  • AlShebli, B. K., Rahwan, T. & Woon, W. L. (2018). The preeminence of ethnic diversity in scientific collaboration. Nature Communications, 9, 5163. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-018-07634-8
  • Clinical Trials Transformation Initiative (2023). CTTI Recommendations: Increasing Diversity in Clinical Trials.
  • Hofstra, B., Kulkarni, V. V., Munoz-Najar Galvez, S., He, B., Jurafsky, D. & McFarland, D. A. (2020). The Diversity–Innovation Paradox in Science. PNAS, 117(17), 9284–9291. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1915378117
  • Nielsen, M. W., Alegria, S., Börjeson, L., Etzkowitz, H., Falk-Krzesinski, H. J., Joshi, A., Leahey, E., Smith-Doerr, L., Woolley, A. W. & Schiebinger, L. (2017). Opinion: Gender diversity leads to better science. PNAS, 114(8), 1740–1742. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1700616114

Additional Material

  • Springer Nature. Supporting DEI in research institutions: supporting researchers (The Link blog).
  • Transcend. How to leverage your DEI strategy for real business impact (infographic: strategic and financial benefits of a diverse workforce).
  • Wiley. Starting points for increasing diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) in your research (infographic).
